Pinfish (Lagodon rhomboides) undergo a complex pelagic larval phase before transitioning to structured seagrass habitats. Field surveys of spawning aggregations in the northern Gulf of Mexico indicate that females release between 250 and 300 eggs per spawning event, and under optimal thermal conditions they can produce a new clutch every four to five days during the peak reproductive season. In laboratory settings, fecundity per event has been recorded at 270 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 270 eggs per clutch], with a spawning frequency of 0.22 clutches per day [F_R_i = 0.22 clutches per day] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 18.8 °C [T = 18.8 °C]. The early developmental milestones are tightly linked to temperature; the incubation period of the fertilised, yolk-laden eggs lasts approximately 48 hours before the onset of larval eclosion. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are initially dependent on endogenous reserves, with the mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding occurring roughly 72 hours post-hatch, a timing that aligns with patterns reported for other sparid teleosts in subtropical waters.

Body size at the transition to sexual maturity represents a critical life-history threshold for this species. Examination of gonadal development in specimens collected from Tampa Bay and adjacent estuaries reveals that puberty is attained at a total length of 13.1 cm [Lp = 13.1 cm], a value that corresponds closely to the size at which the majority of individuals exhibit active gametogenesis. The corresponding wet weight at this developmental stage is 34.4 g [Wwp = 34.4 g], estimated from the length-weight relationship derived from regional stock assessments. These morphometric benchmarks are considerably smaller than the maximum dimensions the species can achieve; the ultimate total length recorded for Lagodon rhomboides is 40 cm [Li = 40 cm], though most individuals encountered in coastal fisheries rarely exceed 25 cm. The wet weight at birth, by contrast, is minuscule: the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, emerging from a pelagic egg with a diameter of approximately 1.02 mm, has an initial mass of only 0.00055 g [Wwb = 0.00055 g], reflecting the limited per-offspring investment characteristic of many broadcast-spawning marine fishes.

Maximum longevity in wild populations of Pinfish has been estimated from otolith-based age validation studies conducted across the southeastern Atlantic and Gulf coasts. The oldest confirmed individual was recorded at 8 years [am = 8 years] of age, a figure that was derived from specimens sampled in relatively stable thermal regimes averaging 18.8 °C [T = 18.8 °C]. This lifespan places Lagodon rhomboides among the longer-lived members of the Sparidae within its size class, although it is notably shorter than that reported for the ecologically similar sheepshead (Archosargus probatocephalus), which can exceed 15 years. The relationship between temperature and senescence is particularly relevant for this species, as it occupies a broad latitudinal gradient spanning from the Yucatán Peninsula to Cape Cod; individuals from northern populations, exposed to cooler annual mean temperatures, may approach the upper end of the recorded lifespan more consistently than their southern conspecifics, which experience accelerated metabolic rates and higher cumulative reproductive output over a compressed period.

The maximum recorded adult body mass for Pinfish is 1020 g [Wwi = 1020 g], a value derived from the length-weight allometry that governs this species and applied to the largest reported total length. This substantial weight is typically associated with large, older females that dominate the spawning biomass in deeper offshore waters, where predation pressure from piscivorous birds and larger teleosts is somewhat reduced. In coastal seagrass meadows, individuals of 300 to 500 g are more commonly encountered, reflecting the spatial segregation by size class that characterizes the species' demography. The mass at first sexual maturity, 34.4 g [Wwp = 34.4 g], represents a 62,500-fold increase over the initial mass at hatching, illustrating the dramatic growth trajectory that takes place during the first year of life. Juvenile fish recruit into Thalassia testudinum beds at around 30 to 40 mm total length, where they feed predominantly on harpacticoid copepods and amphipods before shifting to an increasingly herbivorous diet dominated by epiphytic diatoms and seagrass blades as they grow.

Reproductive activity in Pinfish is strongly seasonal and mediated by water temperature, with the majority of spawning effort concentrated between October and April across most of its range. The maximum daily reproductive rate, expressed as the product of fecundity per spawning event and spawning frequency, corresponds to roughly 246 eggs per day per female when evaluated under the stable thermal conditions of 18.8 °C [T = 18.8 °C]. This level of daily output is relatively high for a sparid of its body size and is indicative of an iteroparous, income-breeding strategy that allows individuals to channel recent foraging gains directly into oocyte production. Batch fecundity scales positively with female mass, and larger individuals may deposit over 350 eggs per clutch during the peak of the spawning season. The protracted spawning window, combined with the production of multiple clutches over several months, ensures that at least a portion of the larval cohort encounters favorable planktonic conditions for growth and survival, a bet-hedging tactic common among coastal marine fishes that face high interannual variability in prey availability and water temperature.
